strengths: Addresses an important problem: exact empirical 0–1 loss minimization for interpretable, low-dimensional linear classifiers.
Provides a concrete enumeration strategy, useful partial-loss pruning, and extensive Haskell listings that make the intended implementation inspectable.
weaknesses: The implementation does not optimize Equation (1). That equation penalizes sign(0), whereas loss01 on page 6 treats every boundary prediction as correct. For one-dimensional observations (1, −1) and (2, +1), the algorithm can return a threshold at 1 with reported loss 0 but actual loss 1; a threshold at 1.5 achieves 0. Although a suitable perturbation could repair this example, no construction of the required classifier is implemented.

The central correctness proof is invalid. Appendix A assumes that greater Hamming distance from an optimal cell’s predictions implies greater error against the true labels. Optimality does not imply this monotonic relationship. The connection between enumerated vertices, realizable boundary-label assignments, and optimal returned parameters requires a new argument.

The claimed O(N^D) runtime is contradicted by the supplied algorithm. With the valid upper bound ub=N, no pruning occurs, and each of the binomial(N,D) completed candidates is ultimately scored on all N observations. This requires at least Ω(N^{D+1}) work for fixed D. Neither an amortized analysis nor timing experiments support the claimed improvement over O(N^{D+1}) methods.

The numerical implementation can report an unattainable optimum even for data in general position. With x=(1, 1+10^-9, 1+2×10^-9) and labels=(+1, −1, +1), the 10^-8 tolerance can turn all predictions into zeros and report loss 0, although every linear threshold makes at least one error. Separately, fitw requires an invertible coordinate matrix, which affine general position does not guarantee; a one-dimensional observation at the origin causes the supplied pivot routine to loop.

The claim of the first polynomial-time exact algorithm for fixed dimension is not substantiated. Classical fixed-dimensional hyperplane-arrangement enumeration, including work already cited in the manuscript, combined with evaluating each realizable dichotomy already yields a polynomial-time procedure. The paper must distinguish its actual contribution from these established results.

The evaluation consists of one error table on five small datasets, with N=80–748 and D=3–6. It provides no runtime or memory measurements, scaling studies, pruning ablations, or comparisons with exact solvers. Consequently, it establishes neither computational efficiency nor independently verified optimality.

Reproducibility and practical claims are insufficiently supported: preprocessing, handling of non-general-position data, baseline hyperparameters, and evaluation splits are unspecified. Without a held-out protocol, the reported loss reductions do not establish improved predictive accuracy; without computational comparisons, they do not justify calling ICE a practical replacement for linear SVMs.
